content: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) refers to a group of chronic, progressive inflammatory conditions affecting the digestive tract, with Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis being the two primary types. Fatigue is a prevalent and debilitating symptom in individuals with IBD, significantly impacting their quality of life. However, the subjective and multifaceted nature of fatigue often complicates its management. Currently, the efficacy and safety of pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatments for fatigue in IBD have not been definitively established through systematic reviews. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the efficacy and safety of various interventions for managing fatigue in IBD. This review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed fatigue as either a primary or secondary outcome. The primary outcome of interest was fatigue, while secondary outcomes included quality of life, adverse events (AEs), serious adverse events (SAEs), and withdrawal due to AEs. Fourteen studies involving 3,741 participants were included in the review, with nine trials investigating pharmacological interventions and five trials examining non-pharmacological approaches. Additionally, 30 ongoing studies were identified, and five studies are awaiting classification. Electroacupuncture Electroacupuncture was evaluated in one RCT involving 27 participants. Fatigue was measured using the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy-Fatigue (FACIT-F) scale, which ranges from 0 to 52, with higher scores indicating less fatigue. At week 8, participants receiving electroacupuncture had an average FACIT-F score that was 8.00 points higher than those receiving no treatment (mean difference [MD] 8.00, 95% confidence interval [CI] 6.45 to 9.55; low-certainty evidence). When compared to sham electroacupuncture, FACIT-F scores were also higher at week 8 (MD 5.10, 95% CI 3.49 to 6.71; low-certainty evidence). However, by week 16, the difference between electroacupuncture and sham electroacupuncture was smaller and less certain (MD 2.60, 95% CI 0.74 to 4.46; low-certainty evidence). No adverse events were reported in the electroacupuncture group, except for one adverse event in the sham electroacupuncture group. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and Solution-Focused Therapy One RCT with 18 participants compared CBT to a fatigue information leaflet. The effects of CBT on fatigue were highly uncertain, as indicated by the results of the Inflammatory Bowel Disease-Fatigue (IBD-F) scale. For section I of the IBD-F scale, the MD was -2.16 (95% CI -6.13 to 1.81), and for section II, the MD was -21.62 (95% CI -45.02 to 1.78; very low-certainty evidence). Similarly, the efficacy of solution-focused therapy on fatigue remains uncertain due to the lack of standard summary data (1 RCT, 98 participants). Physical Activity Advice One trial with a 2x2 factorial design (45 participants) investigated the effects of physical activity advice on fatigue. At week 12, participants who received physical activity advice along with omega-3 supplementation had higher FACIT-F scores compared to those who received no physical activity advice and omega-3 supplementation (MD 6.40, 95% CI -1.80 to 14.60; very low-certainty evidence). Similarly, participants who received physical activity advice along with a placebo had higher FACIT-F scores compared to the control group (MD 9.00, 95% CI 1.64 to 16.36; very low-certainty evidence). Adverse events, primarily gastrointestinal in nature, were similar across groups, although more adverse events were reported in the group receiving no physical activity advice and omega-3 supplementation. Pharmacological Interventions Adalimumab, administered at a dose of 40 mg every other week (eow) for patients with moderately to severely active Crohn's disease who had previously responded to induction therapy, may reduce fatigue. However, the evidence is very uncertain (FACIT-F MD 4.30, 95% CI 1.75 to 6.85; very low-certainty evidence). Participants in the adalimumab group were less likely to experience serious adverse events (odds ratio [OR] 0.56, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.96; moderate-certainty evidence) or withdraw due to adverse events (OR 0.48, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.87; moderate-certainty evidence). Ferric maltol, an oral iron therapy, may slightly increase fatigue, as indicated by lower SF-36 vitality scores in the treatment group compared to the placebo group after 12 weeks of treatment (MD -9.31, 95% CI -17.15 to -1.47; low-certainty evidence). There may be little or no difference in adverse events between the ferric maltol and placebo groups (OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.18; low-certainty evidence). Authors' Conclusions The effects of interventions for managing fatigue in IBD remain uncertain. No definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding the efficacy and safety of these interventions. Further high-quality studies with larger sample sizes are needed to evaluate the potential benefits and risks of therapies. Future research should focus on interventions specifically designed to address fatigue in IBD, targeting selected populations and measuring fatigue as the primary outcome.
